title: Gargi returns: "two questions, like two arrows" — the imperishable (3.8)
hook: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka asked about the thread and the inner controller, the one whose body the earth is. Your line was antaryamin.

Gargi stands up again. Two days ago she was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off, and she sat down. This time she speaks to the whole room first. Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya. As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.
screen: `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN.` → `A WARRIOR STRINGING HIS BOW.` → `TWO QUESTIONS, LIKE TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First arrow. What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows. Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow. And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers. That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without darkness. Without wind, without space. Without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without voice or mind, without breath or mouth, without measure, without inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. Then he says what it does. At the command of this imperishable, Gargi, the sun and moon are held apart. Earth and sky are held apart. Hours, days, months and years are held apart. Rivers run east from the snowy mountains, and others west. And whoever performs rites and austerities for thousands of years without knowing this, it comes to an end. Last time, Gargi asked what holds the worlds of Brahman, as if it were one more thing. This time the answer isn't a thing. It's described almost entirely by what it isn't. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him. None of you will beat him. And she falls silent, on her own terms.
screen: `FIRST ARROW: WOVEN ON SPACE.` · `SECOND ARROW: ON WHAT IS SPACE WOVEN?` · `THE IMPERISHABLE: ONLY WHAT IT ISN'T.` · `BOW TO HIM, AND GO HOME.` · then, large: `NEITHER COARSE NOR FINE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let each thing you notice be named and set down: a sound, not that; a sensation in the knee, not that; a thought, not that. Not coarse, like the chair; not fine, like the thought. Keep setting things down, gently, without looking for what's left, and rest in the room the setting-down makes.
Akshara. The imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The same word means a syllable or a letter, and in Gargi's question, it's what even space is woven on.
Your line: neither coarse nor fine. Next, someone asks how many gods there are. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

original.note: Sanskrit akṣara: a (not) + kṣara (perishing): the imperishable; also a syllable or letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gargi was put in her place.
what it means: she came back, asked better, and drew out the book's great description of the imperishable.
what a scholar hears: akṣara in 3.8.8 is described almost wholly by negations (asthūlam anaṇu, not coarse, not fine); the same word names a syllable.

chat.says: Why does Yajnavalkya describe the imperishable mostly by what it isn't?
options: Because it isn't one more thing; it's what even space is woven on.
Because he didn't know the answer and was stalling to save his head.
Because Gargi asked him to keep the real answer from the room.
chat.meaning: Gargi's second arrow asks what space is woven on. The answer, the akshara, isn't a thing: neither coarse nor fine, without inside or outside.

Gargi.meaning: the woman scholar who rises with two questions, like arrows

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who answers the challengers in Janaka's court

Kashi.meaning: an ancient kingdom, named in Gargi's warrior image

akshara.meaning: the imperishable; the same word means a syllable or letter

Brahman.meaning: the great reality the Upanishads seek to know

notes: The archer simile (3.8.2) and the list of negations (3.8.8) are paraphrased and abbreviated; the list includes 'not red, not moist', omitted here. Confirm.
Rivers flowing east and west from the white (snowy) mountains: 3.8.9. Confirm.
The contrast with Gargi's first question is an interpretive reading, not stated in the text; confirm it is acceptable.
'Falls silent, on her own terms' is the writer's framing of 3.8.12 (tato ha vācaknavy upararāma).
